messages.author: 89abf8a3796a510b
messages.subject: cholesky_decompose!
parts:
Hey guys,

So I finally figured out the cholesky derivatives for our autodiff using Marcus' pattern for f: matrix -> matrix. I implemented both the matrix algebra version (in cholesky_decompose_eigen.hpp) and the scalar version (cholesky_decompose.hpp). The former algo is outlined here: http://mathoverflow.net/questions/150427/the-derivative-of-the-cholesky-factor
and the latter is about halfway through this paper: https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/gilesm/files/NA-08-01.pdf

Frustratingly enough, the scalar version is about as fast wall-time-wise (I tested for 10x10 to 500x500) as the naive autodiff through Eigen's llt. The upside is that it uses about 1/10th of the memory, so I'd probably be able to run a 1000x1000 GP on my machine (albeit very slowly!), whereas I'd max out my RAM with our current version. 

The cholesky_decompose_eigen.hpp version is about 5x slower for 10x10 and likely an order of magnitude slower for bigger matrices because you end up doing a bunch of operations that are on order of dim(input matrix) ^ 3. I haven't tried any of the sparse solvers (you'll see that a bunch of the operations in chain() are sparse), so maybe that would provide a speedup. Right now I'm doing the lower triangular view of a dense matrix and solving in place. Maybe QR would be better? I'm not sure right now. My hunch is that this version has more headroom for improvement, so even if we could get it to be 10% faster than Eigen, it'd be great. The memory usage for this version is also about 1/10th of the naive AD through Eigen's cholesky.

Any thoughts on how we can speed up the Eigen version? 

Rob

Attached is an R file with a make_d1() function based on the accepted answer

http://mathoverflow.net/questions/150427/the-derivative-of-the-cholesky-factor

that does the equivalent of cholesky_decompose_eigen.hpp without a communation matrix, elimination matrix, or Kronecker product. If you have a lower-triangular matrix already, then a lower-triangular solve with the identity matrix is the most efficient way to get its inverse, but we might get some speed improvements from using a sparse solver, particularly if you statically allocate it so that we just have to update its non-zero elements every time the log-posterior is called.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] cholesky_decompose!
parts:
We saw the same thing w.r.t. matrix multiply in that
naively calling Eigen was about the same speed or even
a bit faster than our custom approach, but the custom
approach uses far less memory.

My suspicion is that Eigen's maintaining memory
locality better than we are and that we're spending all
the time in our algorithm pulling from memory to CPU.
This is reinforced by the fact that CppAD, which is normally
slow compared to the other autodiff algorithms is very fast
in this case relative to everything but Stan, and CppAD is
the only other package with the traits defined to tell Eigen
the sizes of autodiff variables so that it can sort out blocking
for memory locality efficiently.

I believe Marcus already had the Giles-style matrix derivatives
for left and right division.

If I understand, there are three systems in play:

1. naive autodiff of Eigen's LLT

2. analytic scalar diff (cholesky_decompose.hpp)

3. analytic matrix diff (cholesky_decompose_eigen.hpp)

* 1 and 2 have the same speed, but 3 is 5x slower.

* 2 and 3 use the same amount of memory, but 1 uses 10x as much.

For an N x N matrix, the amount of memory to store the expression
graph for approach 1 grows as O(N^3). Can it be kept
to O(N^2) for 2 and 3? Peak memory usage is going to be determined
by the LLT algorithm --- is that O(N^2) or O(N^3)? Of course, time's
going to hit O(N^3) whatever we do.

And keep in mind that a huge advantage of doing all of our ops
as doubles is that we can speed things up with GPUs, etc. I
think Eigen's planing around with CUDA implementations.

- Bob
